scope.description: Pilot for the catalog-wide history and collector-texture dossier layer. It proves release-level and card-level shape before scaling to every modeled release and card.
in_scope: Japanese First Expansion Pack / No Rarity launch-family rows
English Base Set as a later crosswalk/reference release
not_claiming: official copy counts unless explicitly sourced

sources.title: Local Japanese pre-English release catalog: First Expansion Pack / No Rarity lab
No Rarity Set Research: launch and product-count synthesis

claims.text: The local catalog records October 20, 1996 as the release date for the Japanese First Expansion Pack / No Rarity lab release family.
The local release model carries 102 launch-family rows while explicitly marking the strict booster product count as 96 and the six basic Energy cards as broader Starter Pack caveats.

The research synthesis frames the Expansion Pack as the first full Pokémon TCG set while noting that earlier non-TCG Pokémon card objects and the first glossy CoroCoro promos predate or sit beside it.

The research synthesis treats the blank lower-right corner as the collector-facing No Rarity marker, while warning that the official confirmation trail is thinner than market confidence can make it sound.

The local release rows identify Charizard, Blastoise, Venusaur, Chansey, Mewtwo, Zapdos, Raichu, and other holos as high-attention early chase anchors by rarity, image provenance, and collector texture.

This release matters because it is where the catalog stops being only a list and starts becoming a market memory: product boundaries, rarity grammar, artists, child retail, and later collector proof all collide in one launch-family object.

steps: Separate the strict 96-card booster checklist from the 102-row launch-family lab model.
For non-Energy No Rarity claims, inspect the lower-right rarity-symbol region row by row.
For basic Energy rows, preserve the Starter Pack caveat rather than treating them as strict booster pulls.
Do not use the release dossier alone as proof that a seller's physical card is a No Rarity copy.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep the 96-vs-102 boundary and the lower-right No Rarity marker visible; this release dossier explains context, not physical-card truth.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Explaining or identifying the Japanese First Expansion Pack / No Rarity launch-family model.

narrative.human_title: The first binder page that became a market
narrative.why_it_matters: This is where Pokémon stops being only screen memory and becomes cardboard ritual: a pack, a corner mark, a missing corner mark, a child opening ten cards, and decades later an agent trying to decide what that little blank space should cost in evidence.

sources.title: Local English WoC release catalog: Base Set
Pokémon TCG API v2 set record: Base
Bulbapedia: Base Set (TCG)

claims.text: The local English WoC catalog records January 9, 1999 as the Base Set release date.
The Pokémon TCG API Base Set record returns printedTotal 102 and total 102 for set id base1.
The local corpus treats English Base Set as a later English reference/crosswalk surface for many Japanese launch-family cards, especially artist and card-identity metadata.
Bulbapedia frames Base Set as the first main expansion outside Japan and as the English-language launch set built from the Japanese Expansion Pack / launch-card lineage.

The local catalog's attention rows for English Base Set include the Kanto starter holos, Mewtwo, Chansey, Raichu, Gyarados, Zapdos, key trainer tools, and energy rows that made the early English game feel complete rather than merely collectible.

The local English Base artist cluster is dominated by Ken Sugimori and Mitsuhiro Arita, with Kagemaru Himeno, Keiji Kinebuchi, and early trainer/energy artists giving the launch binder its mixed character-art, monster-art, and tool-card grammar.

For this project, English Base is both the familiar doorway many collectors learned first and a dangerous resemblance machine: it makes the Japanese launch family emotionally legible while requiring agents to preserve English set, edition, Shadowless, Unlimited, and Japanese-print boundaries.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Base Set, base1, English Base, original English Pokemon cards, Shadowless, First Edition, Unlimited, no expansion symbol, or same art as Japanese Expansion Pack.
special_identification_instructions.summary: English Base Set is the 102-row English launch expansion modeled as base1. Preserve set id, row number, language, and edition/Shadowless evidence before comparing it to Japanese launch cards or later reprints.
steps: Preserve release_family_id en_wotc_base_set_19990109 and Pokemon TCG API set id base1.
Confirm the printed row number and no-expansion-symbol Base Set frame before using this release identity.
Do not treat shared artwork as proof of Japanese Expansion Pack, No Rarity, Base Set 2, Legendary Collection, or later reprint identity.
Keep First Edition, Shadowless, and Unlimited as seller-evidence claims; the release row alone does not determine which physical print variant a seller has.
For price, condition, edition, or authenticity claims, use seller-controlled images, graded-label/cert evidence when present, and market evidence; do not infer from catalog memory.

narrative.human_title: The doorway most collectors learned first
narrative.why_it_matters: English Base is where a huge part of the English-speaking world learned the shape of Pokemon cards: the Charizard gravity, the starter trio, the trainers that taught the game, the energy floor, the Ken Sugimori and Mitsuhiro Arita visual grammar. In this catalog it is useful, beloved, and dangerous. It helps an agent explain why an older Japanese row feels familiar, but it must never let familiarity become provenance. English Base is a doorway, not a shortcut.
not_claiming: English Base is the same object as Japanese Expansion Pack

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API identify Mewtwo as English Base Set row base1-10 / printed number 10.
The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API classify Mewtwo base1-10 as a Rare Holo Pokemon card.
The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API credit Ken Sugimori as the illustrator for Mewtwo base1-10.
The Pokemon TCG API payload models Mewtwo base1-10 as a Level 53 Psychic Basic Pokemon with HP 60, Psychic weakness, retreat cost 3, and the attacks Psychic and Barrier.

Mewtwo base1-10 matters because it brought the franchise's laboratory myth into the English launch binder as a holo rather than a side-story: the flavor text, Barrier, and psychic type made the card feel dangerous even beside the starter icons.

Agents should distinguish Mewtwo base1-10 from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity Mewtwo, Base Set 2 Mewtwo, Legendary Collection Mewtwo, Expedition Mewtwo, movie/Wizards promo Mewtwo, and Japanese P Promotional Mewtwo 046/P; the English Base row number, set id base1, Rare Holo status, Ken Sugimori credit, and edition/Shadowless evidence are load-bearing.

Do not infer First Edition, Shadowless, or Unlimited status from this catalog row; require seller scan or graded-label/cert evidence for that variant claim.
Separate this row from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity Mewtwo, Base Set 2 Mewtwo, Legendary Collection Mewtwo, Expedition Mewtwo, movie/Wizards promo Mewtwo, and P Promotional Mewtwo 046/P.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Base Set Mewtwo is the English launch holo that made the laboratory legend feel heavy in a binder: Sugimori image, Psychic/Barrier text, and holo surface all before any seller-specific variant claim.

narrative.human_title: Mewtwo #10: the lab myth in the launch binder
narrative.why_it_matters: Base Set Mewtwo does not need to be the loudest card in the room to change the room. Charizard is spectacle; Mewtwo is unease. Sugimori's image, the stark Psychic/Barrier play pattern, and the flavor of engineered power made the English launch binder feel like it contained something older and colder than a starter evolution. For an agent, that feeling is useful only if the rails stay visible: base1-10 first, edition evidence second, condition and authenticity only after seller proof.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Base Set Venusaur is the English launch holo where Arita's starter-line art meets a real game engine: Energy Trans makes the big plant feel like infrastructure, not just a trophy.

narrative.human_title: Venusaur #15: the launch binder's living engine
narrative.why_it_matters: Base Set Venusaur is easy to undersell if the room is only talking about Charizard. But Venusaur is one of the cards that makes the first English set feel alive. Arita gives it weight and bloom; Energy Trans gives it a job. It is the starter holo that turns Grass energy into motion across the board, which is exactly the kind of assembly this catalog is trying to preserve: art, character, game text, and collector memory all braided into one object. For an agent, the order matters: base1-15 first, edition evidence second, condition and authenticity only after seller proof.

narrative.human_title: Blastoise #2: the launch binder's pressure system
narrative.why_it_matters: Base Set Blastoise is not just the Water starter standing next to Charizard. It is one of the early game's machines. Sugimori gives it the armored-cannon silhouette everyone remembers, and Rain Dance gives that silhouette a mechanism: Water Energy floods the board, Hydro Pump turns the pressure into damage, and suddenly the big turtle is not only a collection icon but a way the game teaches acceleration. For an agent, the feeling is useful only with rails: base1-2 first, edition evidence second, condition and authenticity only after seller proof.

narrative.human_title: Charizard #4: the launch binder's gravity well
narrative.why_it_matters: Base Set Charizard is the card that can distort the whole room. It is Arita's dragon in flight, 120 HP, Energy Burn, Fire Spin, the childhood memory, the auction headline, the card everyone thinks they know. That is exactly why the catalog has to be disciplined. The feeling matters; the assembly matters more. This row is English Base Set base1-4 first, edition evidence second, condition and authenticity only after seller proof. Let the grail glow, but do not let the glow become provenance.

sources.title: Local No Rarity launch-family row: Bulbasaur
Pokémon TCG API English Base Set Bulbasaur card record

claims.text: The local catalog anchors Bulbasaur as Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity lab row PMCG1-001.
The local row imports Mitsuhiro Arita as illustrator from English Base Set crosswalk metadata while warning that this is not direct Japanese-print proof.
The local row models Bulbasaur as a Common, Basic Grass Pokémon with National Pokédex number 1.
Bulbasaur matters in this pilot because it is the opening row: the first catalog position turns a modest common into a test of whether the agent can care about more than grails.
Inside the pilot, Arita's credit appears across Bulbasaur, Pikachu, and Charizard, which makes him a connective artist for the launch-family story rather than a one-card footnote.

narrative.why_it_matters: Bulbasaur is not the loudest card in the room, which is exactly why it belongs in the first pilot. If the catalog can make PMCG1-001 feel alive without inflating it into a chase myth, the voice is learning restraint.

narrative.human_title: The magazine insert before the pack
narrative.why_it_matters: This is the kind of card that makes the project worth doing. It is not just Pikachu; it is CoroCoro, timing, glossy paper, source conflict, and the messy way a culture becomes collectible before the tidy checklist arrives.
